title: Facet-selective ballistic supercurrent in a weak topological insulator
why_careful: Three junctions with two superconductors (Al, NbN) and two crystal orientations, two field orientations on the same junction, STM evidence for the bulk gap and step-edge states, temperature dependence of Ic, and simulated interference patterns that bound what the current-density reconstruction can resolve.

spans:
This facet selectivity is robust across multiple devices and two dif-
ferent superconductors (Al and NbN), and its topological origin is further supported
by a striking dependence on magnetic-field orientation.

First, SQUID-
like patterns appear for two separate Al/ZrTe5 devices. Moreover, a NbN/ZrTe5 junction
oriented along the c-axis produces SQUID-like oscillations (Fig. 5a,b), demonstrating
reproducibility across different superconductors and crystallographic orientations.

The reproducibility across two
superconductors (Al and NbN), two junction orientations (along the a- and c-axes), and
three independent devices suggests that our results originate from intrinsic properties
of ZrTe5 , rather than from device-specific artifacts.
info.why: these are the only statements of how many devices show the SQUID-like pattern and that the effect is not device-specific

spans:
However, the extracted widths are upper bounds on the intrinsic width
of the localized channels [43], because the Fourier-based reconstruction is limited by the
finite magnetic-field range of the measured interference pattern. As shown in Supplemen-
tary Fig. S7, even for an ideal SQUID interference pattern, the extracted supercurrent
peaks have finite widths. Thus, the reconstructed supercurrent density profile reliably
identifies where the supercurrent predominantly flows, but does not by itself provide
a precise quantitative measure of the intrinsic width or magnitude of the supercurrent
peaks [43].
info.why: states that the Fourier reconstruction of Js(x) is limited by the measured field range and that even an ideal SQUID pattern gives finite peak widths
